explanation: Three months after blunt trauma, persistent blood in the anterior chamber and angle with an IOP of 33 mm Hg points to a red-cell-related secondary glaucoma - ghost cell glaucoma from degenerated erythrocytes migrating forward from the vitreous, or a haemolytic picture - in which the trabecular meshwork is mechanically obstructed by cells and macrophages. Observation is not defensible at this pressure after this long, and pilocarpine is the wrong drug class: miotics do little for an obstructed meshwork and are relatively contraindicated after blunt trauma with angle recession because they can worsen outflow and stir up inflammation. Anterior chamber washout, with removal of the vitreous reservoir if that is the source, is the definitive step once medical therapy fails or the pressure has been this high for this long. In real practice aqueous suppressants would be started first, which is why this key should be read with caution.
concern: Option C is absent from the recall (the letters jump A, B, D) and the standard first-line answer, topical aqueous suppressants, is very likely the option that was lost. The gonioscopy image could not be reviewed.

explanation: A spontaneous vitreous haemorrhage in a diabetic eye is proliferative disease until proved otherwise, since neovascular tissue bleeding into the vitreous is the only common diabetic mechanism; severe NPDR by definition has no new vessels and cannot bleed into the vitreous, and calling it idiopathic ignores the risk profile in front of you. High-risk PDR is a defined entity from the Diabetic Retinopathy Study - NVD of at least a quarter to a third of a disc area, any NVD with preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage, or NVE of at least half a disc area with haemorrhage - and establishing it requires visible neovascularisation. Because the blood obscures the retina and no new vessels are documented, the defensible label is PDR; the eye is followed with serial B-scan and given panretinal photocoagulation as soon as a view returns.
concern: Some examiners treat any vitreous haemorrhage in a diabetic as evidence of high-risk PDR, so option D is a live alternative.

explanation: Untreated polyarteritis nodosa carries a 5-year survival of roughly 13 percent, and corticosteroid treatment raises that to about half, with cyclophosphamide pushing it higher still. That makes the statement that treated patients have roughly a 50 percent 5-year survival the classic teaching figure. Death within a year of diagnosis describes only the most fulminant untreated cases rather than the rule, and ocular involvement is not itself the prognostic driver: renal, cardiac, gastrointestinal and central nervous system involvement are what determine survival in this vasculitis.
concern: Option B carries a stray parenthetical about relapse risk that appears to belong to option D, and option D (steroids reduce relapse) is arguably also true, which softens the item.

explanation: Prism before either eye acts on the vergence demand of the pair, so a required amount of base-out can be divided between the two eyes, and 3 prism dioptres base-out over the right eye is conventionally split as 1.5 base-out before each eye. Splitting is preferred because it halves the peripheral distortion, chromatic aberration, image displacement and cosmetic thickness that a single large prism produces. Base-in before the fellow eye would not be equivalent: base-out right combined with base-in left puts both bases toward the same side of space, giving a yoked or version prism that shifts both images together and leaves the vergence demand unchanged.
concern: Option C reads '1.5 bo od and 1.5 bi os'; the 'bi' is almost certainly a transcription slip for 'bo', since only an equal base-out split is equivalent. Taken literally, no option is correct.

explanation: Two months after herpes zoster ophthalmicus, redness, photophobia and blurred vision with an intact epithelium is the classic picture of zoster stromal keratitis or anterior uveitis, both immune-mediated and both treated with a topical corticosteroid such as prednisolone acetate on a slow taper, usually with oral antiviral cover in the earlier phase. Trifluridine and ganciclovir gel are directed at active epithelial viral replication, and trifluridine in particular is frankly toxic to the epithelium with prolonged use; there is no epithelial defect here to treat. Ciprofloxacin addresses bacterial keratitis, which does not fit an intact epithelium or this time course.

Management of a pigmented conjunctival lesion turns entirely on its appearance, location and behaviour. A stable, well-circumscribed juvenile nevus containing intralesional cysts is documented photographically and observed, whereas primary acquired melanosis with atypia or a nodular lesion with feeder vessels needs wide excision using a no-touch technique with cryotherapy to the conjunctival margins and alcohol epitheliectomy for any corneal component. Without the photograph neither option can be chosen.
concern: The stem refers to a picture but no image is attached to this recall, and the answer depends completely on the appearance of the lesion.

explanation: Aciclovir has an oral bioavailability of only about 10 to 20 percent, and topical antivirals penetrate the cornea poorly, so inadequate drug concentration at the target tissue, compounded by the five-times-daily dosing burden and the poor adherence that follows, is the usual reason herpetic ocular disease fails to respond. This is precisely why valaciclovir and famciclovir, with far better absorption, were developed. True antiviral resistance from thymidine kinase-deficient mutants is well described but rare outside immunocompromised hosts, hepatic clearance is not a limiting factor at standard doses, and allergy leads to drug discontinuation rather than to treatment failure.
concern: Some question banks key this as viral resistance, so the item is arguable.

explanation: A diabetic vitreous haemorrhage with an attached retina on B-scan is followed rather than operated on: most such haemorrhages clear enough over weeks to allow panretinal photocoagulation, and serial ultrasound is what guards against tractional detachment developing behind the blood. Vitrectomy becomes the answer when the haemorrhage fails to clear, when ultrasound shows traction threatening or involving the macula, or in a type 1 diabetic with dense bilateral haemorrhage where earlier surgery has been shown to help. YAG hyaloidotomy is a technique for a discrete premacular subhyaloid haemorrhage, not for diffuse vitreous blood, and anti-VEGF may hasten clearing but is an adjunct rather than the defined next step.

As transcribed the stem cannot be reconstructed. If the question is which change improves retinoscopic accuracy, a longer working distance reduces the dioptric consequence of misjudging that distance: being 5 cm out at 50 cm introduces about a quarter of a dioptre of error, while the same 5 cm at 67 cm introduces roughly half that, although the reflex dims and neutrality becomes harder to judge. Saying the working distance makes no difference is simply wrong, since its dioptric value is subtracted from the gross retinoscopy result.
concern: The stem ('his cyclorefration in 50cm was clear, what you make your retinoscopy accuracy') is garbled past the point where the question being asked can be identified, and the options are elliptical.

explanation: A +14 add puts the reading material about 7 cm from the eyes, a convergence demand of roughly 30 prism dioptres, far beyond what almost anyone can sustain; worse, converging eyes look through the nasal part of a strong plus lens, which adds a base-out prismatic effect and increases the demand further. Fusion breaks down into a manifest exodeviation after sustained near work, which is why high-add low-vision readers are dispensed with base-in prism incorporated or with one eye occluded. Esophoria is the wrong direction, since the induced effect is a convergence burden rather than an excess of convergence, and diplopia is the symptom that follows the exodeviation rather than its cause.
concern: The stem is garbled and it is unclear whether the examiners wanted the mechanism (exodeviation) or the resulting symptom, so option C is a live alternative.

explanation: Moving a minus correction from the spectacle plane onto the cornea abolishes the vertex distance, and for a myope that increases the accommodative demand at near: the spectacle-corrected myope enjoys a reduced accommodative requirement which disappears in contact lenses. The same shift also removes the base-in prismatic help that minus spectacles provide when the eyes converge, so convergence demand rises too. A keratoconic moved into rigid gas permeable lenses therefore gains distance acuity from the regularised anterior surface while finding near work harder. A rigid lens does not induce base-out prism in this setting, and depth of focus is if anything better with the sharper retinal image the contact lens delivers.

A comfortable near add leaves half the amplitude of accommodation in reserve. At 50 cm the demand is 2.00 D; with an amplitude of only 1.50 D the patient can comfortably sustain 0.75 D, so the add required is 2.00 minus 0.75, which is +1.25 D. That figure matches the compiler's note but is not among the numbered choices offered, so the only correct choice is the placeholder option.
concern: The correct value (+1.25) is not among options A, B or C, and the only correct choice is option D, whose text is the placeholder 'Other number I don't recall'. The item cannot ship until the real option D is recovered.

explanation: Contact lenses are the classical optical choice in congenital nystagmus: they move with the eye so the correction stays centred whatever the eye position, and lid and corneal contact appears to dampen the nystagmus through trigeminal afferent feedback, improving acuity beyond the purely refractive effect. Spectacles in a nystagmus patient with an eccentric null point force viewing through the lens periphery, adding prismatic and aberrational error. Ptosis is the one situation where spectacles are actually preferred, since a ptosis crutch mounts on the frame, and a face turn from strabismus is usually managed with prism or surgery rather than by changing lens modality.
concern: Option A is a reasonable alternative, since an anomalous head posture also degrades spectacle optics.

explanation: Classic galactosemia is autosomal recessive and results from deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase, so both recalled statements are true and the exception the examiners wanted must lie among the options that were lost. The oil-droplet cataract arises from galactitol accumulating through aldose reductase and can reverse on a galactose-free diet if caught early, and the galactokinase-deficient variant produces cataract without the systemic hepatic, renal and neurological disease.
concern: Only two options survive and both are correct statements, so the answer to this EXCEPT question is not present.

explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma spreads superiorly through the foramen lacerum into the petroclival region and cavernous sinus, where the abducens nerve has the longest and most exposed intracranial course, so a sixth nerve palsy is the commonest cranial neuropathy and is often the presenting sign in a patient whose nasal symptoms have been dismissed. Trigeminal involvement is the next most frequent and produces the classic numb cheek from maxillary division compression, but it trails the sixth. Facial and vestibulocochlear deficits occur late and usually reflect extensive skull base disease or treatment effect, and the ear symptom that actually brings these patients in is a conductive loss from a middle ear effusion rather than a true eighth nerve palsy.

All three recalled statements are defensible. Staphylococcal keratitis classically gives a round or oval, well-demarcated grey-white stromal infiltrate with relatively clear surrounding stroma; a descemetocele means the stroma has melted away leaving only Descemet membrane, so perforation is imminent and it is a surgical emergency; and gram-negative rods, along with Pseudomonas, Acanthamoeba and fungi, are described causes of a ring infiltrate. With no false statement among the surviving options, the item cannot be keyed.
concern: This is a 'one false' item in which all three recalled options read as true, so the false option appears to have been lost.

explanation: Microspherophakia is the signature lens abnormality of Weill-Marchesani syndrome, and the short stature with stubby fingers described in the second option is simply the habitus of that same syndrome, so neither of those can be the exception. Standard paediatric ophthalmology sources also list Alport syndrome and Lowe syndrome among microspherophakia associations, alongside Marfan syndrome, hyperlysinaemia, congenital rubella and Peters anomaly, even though the more characteristic lens lesion is anterior lenticonus in Alport and a dense disc-shaped congenital cataract in Lowe.
concern: Options A and B name the same syndrome, and both remaining candidates are listed associations in standard texts, so no single defensible exception exists among the recalled options.

explanation: Conservative management of a bleb leak is aqueous suppression to reduce flow through the defect, a prophylactic topical antibiotic against blebitis, a large-diameter bandage contact lens or symblepharon ring to tamponade the leak, and reduction or withdrawal of topical corticosteroid so the conjunctival epithelium can heal; if those fail, autologous blood injection, cyanoacrylate glue or surgical revision follow. What is applied mechanically is a pressure patch, since a loose or light patch does nothing to appose the leaking edges, which makes that the odd one out.
concern: This is a soft item. 'Light patch' may be a transcription of 'tight patch' or 'pressure patch', in which case all four options are legitimate management steps. The compiler's hint pointed to the bandage contact lens, which is unambiguously a standard treatment, so I have diverged from it.

explanation: The stem has been overwritten by an unrelated sentence about remission induction in systemic vasculitis and is then cut off mid-word, so what the options are meant not to affect cannot be determined. If the intended endpoint was duration of local anaesthesia, then site of injection, volume or dose given, and the vascularity of the tissue all influence how long the block lasts, whereas alkalinisation with bicarbonate mainly accelerates onset by increasing the un-ionised fraction available to cross the nerve membrane.

The surviving options suggest an item about acute-phase markers, most plausibly in giant cell arteritis, where ESR and CRP are both typically raised and the two together give better sensitivity than either alone, but nothing here can be keyed.

explanation: Lattice degeneration is common, present in something like 8 to 10 percent of the population, and the overwhelming majority of lattice eyes never detach, so a figure of a third progressing to rhegmatogenous detachment is far too high; the roughly one in three figure belongs to the converse statement, that about a quarter to a third of detachments occur in eyes with lattice. Prophylactic retinopexy for asymptomatic lattice, with or without atrophic round holes, has not been shown to reduce detachment risk in a phakic eye without other risk factors and is generally not advised. Treatment is indicated when a posterior vitreous detachment produces a symptomatic break with persistent vitreoretinal traction on its edge, which is the situation option D describes.
concern: Options A and B have been merged into a single option A, so the reader sees a false statement and a roughly true one under the same letter; the options should be split before this ships. The stem is also entirely bleed-through text about Purtscher-like retinopathy and must be replaced with the real lattice degeneration stem.

explanation: Actinic or solar keratosis is the premalignant epithelial eyelid lesion: it arises on chronically sun-exposed skin, shows epidermal dysplasia histologically and can progress to squamous cell carcinoma, which is why it is excised or treated rather than watched indefinitely. Seborrhoeic keratosis, inverted follicular keratosis and squamous papilloma are all benign epithelial proliferations without meaningful malignant potential, although an irritated seborrhoeic keratosis or an inverted follicular keratosis can look alarming both clinically and under the microscope and is a recognised source of overdiagnosis.
concern: The options were merged during extraction: option A's text contains both 'Seborrheic keratosis' and 'Actinic keratosis', and option C contains both 'Inverted follicular keratosis' and 'Papilloma'. The correct answer has no letter key of its own, so the item must be re-split before it can ship.

explanation: Knudson's two-hit model requires both copies of RB1 at 13q14 to be inactivated before a retinoblastoma develops, and survivors of the heritable form carry that first hit in every cell, which is why they face a lifetime excess of second malignancies, particularly osteosarcoma, soft tissue sarcoma, melanoma and pinealoblastoma. What the ocular classifications do not predict is patient survival: Reese-Ellsworth was built to predict globe salvage after external beam radiotherapy and the International Classification of Retinoblastoma predicts eye preservation with chemoreduction. Survival is driven by extraocular extension, optic nerve invasion beyond the lamina cribrosa and metastasis, which is what the separate International Retinoblastoma Staging System addresses.
concern: The stem is preceded by bleed-through text about lens dislocation in homocystinuria that should be stripped before shipping.

explanation: Only the tail of this item survives. The three statements all describe amplitude of accommodation: it is driven by parasympathetic innervation reaching the ciliary muscle through the ciliary ganglion and short ciliary nerves, it measures roughly 4 to 8 dioptres at age 40 by Hofstetter's formulae, and it is exactly why a resident who accommodates at the operating microscope keeps losing focus. So 'all of the above' is the intended answer, but neither the stem nor that option survives in usable form.
concern: There is no question stem at all; the field contains only contaminating tonometry text and a question number. Option D ('All of the above') has been merged into option C's text, so the correct answer has no letter key.

explanation: Nothing of the real stem survives; the text shown belongs to a different question about Peters anomaly and its chromosomal associations. The options read like a phlyctenulosis item: a corneal phlyctenule begins at or near the limbus, may migrate centrally dragging a leash of vessels behind it, and heals leaving a triangular scar with its base at the limbus, so 'most commonly affects the central cornea' would be the false statement. Without the stem, even the polarity of the question is unknown, and a true-statement version would key differently.

explanation: On the traditional anatomical classification Reis-Bucklers is a Bowman layer or anterior dystrophy, while granular, lattice and macular are the classic stromal dystrophies, which makes Reis-Bucklers the odd one out. The IC3D scheme complicates the picture by grouping Reis-Bucklers with Thiel-Behnke, lattice and granular as epithelial-stromal TGFBI dystrophies, leaving macular dystrophy, a CHST6 keratan sulphate disorder, as the only true stromal dystrophy of the four. Either way the intended answer is Reis-Bucklers, but the examinee needs to know which classification is being tested.
concern: Options were merged during extraction (A carries both Reis-Bucklers and granular; C carries lattice and macular) and option C's text also contains a commentary that states the answer outright. The item leaks its own key and needs rebuilding from the source page.

explanation: Any canalicular laceration should be repaired if at all possible, with fine apposition of the pericanalicular tissue over a silicone stent; the upper canaliculus is not disposable, since a proportion of patients drain preferentially through it and an unrepaired upper system can leave epiphora and lid notching. Repair is ideally performed within 24 to 48 hours, but delayed repair days later remains feasible, because the cut medial edge can usually be identified by careful inspection under magnification, probing, or irrigating the opposite punctum until fluid or air appears at the cut end, so the claim that repair becomes impossible after 72 hours is far too absolute. Canalicular lacerations follow dog bites, hooks and blunt medial lid avulsion; they are not markers of fatal injury and they are certainly not repaired only when the lower canaliculus is also cut.
concern: The stem is preceded by bleed-through text about inferior oblique actions. This answer diverges from the compiler's hint of B, which overstates the Kanski timing advice as an absolute cut-off.

The list is recognisable as tests used to probe macular function when the media are hazy or the acuity is unexplained: blue-field entoptoscopy, laser interferometry and two-point discrimination all assess the fovea's capacity to resolve, whereas colour vision testing is a broader measure that is more informative about optic nerve disease. Both the polarity and the wording of the question are gone, so nothing can be keyed with confidence.

There is no answerable content.

explanation: Drug leaves the vitreous by two routes: anteriorly, diffusing into the posterior and then anterior chamber to exit with aqueous through the conventional outflow pathways, and posteriorly, across the retina and retinal pigment epithelium, a route that includes active transport of organic anions such as the penicillins. Trans-scleral movement is a minor pathway and is not the main route of elimination, which makes that the false statement. The other three hold up: melanin in the uvea and pigment epithelium binds many drugs and prolongs their intraocular residence, active outward transport across the retina is real, and breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier floods the eye with protein that binds drug and reduces the free, pharmacologically active fraction.
concern: This diverges from the compiler's hint of A. Option A's phrase 'drug inactivity' is loosely worded, so the item remains arguable.

explanation: Corneal epithelial healing runs through a latent phase, a migration phase and only then a proliferative phase: cells at the leading edge flatten, dissolve their hemidesmosomes and slide across the defect, and mitosis at that leading edge is actually suppressed while migration is under way, with proliferation occurring behind the front and at the limbal stem cell niche. That makes the claim about mitosis at the wound edge the false statement. Fibronectin deposited on the wound bed is a well-established promoter of epithelial adhesion, spreading and healing, low-dose ultraviolet exposure has long been described as stimulating epithelial mitosis while larger doses inhibit it, and adrenergic agents that raise intracellular cyclic AMP, epinephrine among them, retard epithelial migration and division.
concern: Option A is transcribed as 'Miosis' with a trailing question mark; if the original word was not 'mitosis' the meaning of the option changes.

explanation: Oscillatory potentials are the small high-frequency wavelets riding on the ascending limb of the b-wave, and they are generated in the inner plexiform layer, principally by amacrine cell feedback circuitry. They are among the earliest electroretinographic abnormalities in diabetic retinopathy and in central retinal vein occlusion, both inner retinal ischaemic conditions, which is the clinical reason to know them. The retinal pigment epithelium generates the c-wave and the light rise of the electro-oculogram, horizontal cells contribute to the slow PIII and to shaping the b-wave rather than to the oscillations, and ganglion cells are essentially silent on the full-field ERG, appearing instead in the pattern ERG and the photopic negative response.

Retinoscopy measures the eye's refraction relative to the examiner's position, so the dioptric value of the working distance must be subtracted from the gross finding. A working distance of 67 cm corresponds to 1.50 D; neutralising with no lens in the trial frame means the gross result is plano and the net refraction is minus 1.50 D. Answering plano ignores the working distance correction altogether, and a plus answer applies that correction in the wrong direction.
concern: The options are written without signs; the intended answer is minus 1.50 D.

explanation: The meibomian glands are modified sebaceous glands embedded in the tarsal plate, so obstruction of one and the sterile lipogranulomatous inflammation that follows is a chalazion, a firm, painless, deeply seated nodule best appreciated on lid eversion. An external hordeolum, the common stye, is an acute staphylococcal infection of the glands of Zeis or Moll at the lash line, superficial and pointing anteriorly through the skin. The meibomian counterpart of a stye is the internal hordeolum, an acute infection of the meibomian gland pointing through the tarsal conjunctiva, which is what distinguishes it from the chronic, non-infectious chalazion.

Hering's law of equal innervation is the law of yoked muscles and belongs with conjugate version movements rather than being a property peculiar to vergence; convergence, not version, is the eye movement component of the near triad alongside accommodation and pupillary miosis; and it is retinal disparity that drives fusional vergence, whereas version is driven by displacement of the fixation target. That leaves the corpus callosum statement, and interhemispheric transfer through the callosum does contribute to binocular fusion and vergence control, particularly for stimuli straddling the vertical meridian.
concern: Every distractor carries the compiler's own correction in parentheses ('X version', 'X vergence is part of near triad'), which tells the reader outright which options are false. The item is salvageable only if those annotations are stripped from the option text.

explanation: The vortex veins drain the uveal venous circulation, meaning choroid, ciliary body and iris, and they exit through oblique scleral canals a few millimetres behind the equator, where their ampullae are readily seen on indirect ophthalmoscopy of the mid-periphery. The retina drains through the central retinal vein, which leaves the eye within the optic nerve, so the statement that vortex veins drain the retina is the incorrect one. There are typically four to seven, roughly one or two per quadrant, and their number and position matter surgically because scleral buckling or drainage of subretinal fluid close to an ampulla risks choroidal haemorrhage or effusion.

Household bleach, sodium hypochlorite, has a pH around 11 to 12 and is one of the commoner domestic alkalis to reach the eye, alongside ammonia in cleaning products, lye in drain cleaner and lime in cement and plaster. The other options invert established facts: a pH above 7 is alkaline rather than acidic, and alkalis are more destructive than acids because they saponify cell membrane lipids and penetrate rapidly into stroma and anterior chamber, whereas acids coagulate surface protein and to some extent barricade themselves out. Severity depends on concentration, volume and contact time as well as pH, so setting pH against concentration is a false dichotomy.
concern: Option C is a live alternative if the examiners intended the teaching that pH predicts severity better than the identity of the agent, and some texts describe bleach as causing only mild ocular injury.

explanation: The corneal stroma is built predominantly of type I collagen fibrils, with type V co-assembled into those fibrils to regulate their uniformly small diameter and type VI forming the filamentous network of the interfibrillar matrix; that uniform fibril diameter and regular lattice spacing, held by the proteoglycans, is what keeps the stroma transparent. Type IV is the basement membrane collagen of the epithelial and endothelial basal laminae, type VIII is the major collagen of Descemet membrane, and types II and III are cartilage and reticular collagens with no meaningful role in the normal adult stroma, which rules out the other three combinations.

Lens transparency depends on the crystallins being water-soluble and packed at very high concentration in short-range order, so that scattered light cancels by destructive interference; when they aggregate into high-molecular-weight water-insoluble complexes, light scatters and cataract results, which means calling the crystallins insoluble reverses the physiology. The other statements hold: the fetal nucleus carries an upright Y suture anteriorly and an inverted Y posteriorly, secondary lens fibres are generated throughout life from the epithelial cells at the equatorial bow, and the lens epithelium is a single cuboidal layer confined to the anterior surface beneath the capsule.

Type 1 diabetes has a datable onset and clinically significant retinopathy essentially does not appear within the first five years, so the first dilated fundus examination is recommended five years after diagnosis, with annual review thereafter. Type 2 diabetes is the opposite case: the onset date is unknown and a substantial minority already have retinopathy when the diagnosis is made, so screening begins immediately. Examining a newly diagnosed type 1 patient yields nothing, and the paediatric caveat is worth remembering, since screening is generally deferred until the child is around ten years old or has entered puberty, whichever comes first.

Brown syndrome is a restriction of elevation in adduction caused by a tight, short or non-sliding superior oblique tendon-trochlea complex; adduction itself is full, which makes 'mainly adduction defect' the false statement. The forced duction test is positive, demonstrating mechanical resistance to elevating the adducted eye, and that finding is what separates Brown syndrome from inferior oblique palsy, in which forced ductions are free. Acquired Brown syndrome from trauma, trochleitis or an inflammatory arthropathy reflects swelling of the tendon or its sheath at the trochlea, may be intermittent, and is sometimes accompanied by a palpable or audible click.

Yoke muscles are the pair that carry the two eyes together into a given field of gaze, and the vertical pairings are right superior rectus with left inferior oblique, right inferior rectus with left superior oblique, right superior oblique with left inferior rectus, and right inferior oblique with left superior rectus. Pairing the right superior oblique with the left inferior oblique is therefore the false combination: the right superior oblique depresses the adducted right eye in down-and-left gaze, where its yoke is the left inferior rectus, while the left inferior oblique elevates the adducted left eye in up-and-right gaze, where its yoke is the right superior rectus. The remaining three combinations are correct, including the horizontal pair of right lateral rectus with left medial rectus for right gaze.
